先说结论，我推荐这款游戏是因为我的个人喜好，个人评分7/10。
我本人是打折入手的，9+8.2+5.6，合计22.8人民币，不是很推荐原价入手（可以去看看另一个Fishing: North Atlantic，都是同一个制作组的游戏，那个比较新一些，等不及要买的话可以去试试它），那个价位哪怕对爱好者也太高了，当然你是有钱人的话另说。
……
先说不好的地方：

①如果你是奔着海钓之类的想法，那么这款游戏不适合你。它没有钓鱼功能，即使是游戏初期也用的是延绳钓，没有甩鱼竿的玩法。

②这游戏的中文不说全部，但是有相当一部分是机器翻译，而且有些地方的翻译是错的。不过总体上容易入门的。

③这游戏的玩法非常少，比较重要的玩法只有一种，就是出海→放设备→回港→等→出海→收设备→回港，如此循环。在这个过程里，小型渔船、中型渔船、大型渔船和远洋渔船（必须提醒游戏内没有这个分类，实际上是按照许可证分的，即业余→初级→高级→船长）的操作有少许区别，但总体没变，中型船只以上可以雇佣船员帮你干活。如果你买了帝王蟹DLC，则多了一种区别更大的玩法就是钓帝王蟹。不过要注意的是，游戏里只有一艘中型船和一艘大型船可以装蟹笼。

④结合上一条，该游戏没有任何随机事件，同时也没有其他消耗金钱的地方，也就是说在后期采购所有船只和所有升级之后，赚钱就没有意义了。此时还能支持我进游戏的动力，就是悠哉地在船上看着船员忙碌，欣赏一下风景。接受不了这个的话，这个游戏对你最多只有48小时的游戏时长。

⑤截止到现在的2026年1月，该游戏依然会偶尔闪退，记得随时存档。
……
接下来是一些玩法和建议：

1、贷款功能很好用，只要贷款后能买到下一个规格的船（小→中→大→远洋）就直接买，高规格的船舶单次出海的收益高，必然能在较短的时间内把你的贷款补回来，但需要注意两点，第一要记得随时存档，方便在花钱过度的时候回档，第二要确认贷款买船后有多余的钱采购渔具，最好多留二十万kr到三十万kr。

2、帝王蟹DLC最好买一下，毕竟你都愿意掏钱买这个游戏了，那另外两个DLC（特别是帝王蟹DLC）估计也会适合你。

3、虽然游戏里的快速旅行功能无法选择你放下的渔具附近一百米的位置，但是你可以在渔具后面标点，让你的船和标点之间的线段穿过渔具，然后掐准时机停止快速旅行，就能停在距离渔具更近的位置上。

4、我个人是把游戏里的船舶分成四个等级，即小型渔船，中型渔船，大型渔船和远洋渔船。
小型渔船：价格在十多万kr左右，无法携带船员，外观类似于快艇。
中型渔船：价格在数十万kr左右，除Fix之外均可携带极少量船员。
大型渔船：价格在数百万kr左右，大型和远洋渔船都能带五名以上的船员。
远洋渔船：价格在一千万kr以上。

5、要注意船的升级是跟船的，包括渔具也一样。比如你在初始的Borge上买过一百米长的延绳，这根绳子没法跟着你去其他船，即使那艘船也能用一百米的延绳。但像是鱼钩、望远镜这些设备则是跟角色的，换别的船也能用。

6、捕蟹船总共有两款，分别是Selfy和Svalbard，前者可以分别游玩延绳钓、渔网和蟹笼（要回港口切换），但后者只能用来捕蟹。

7、我本人的买船路线是Borge（小）→Selfy（中）→Svalbard（大），要注意虽然Yazzy和Tobie都是小型船，但Selfy这艘中型船的价格其实比Tobie更便宜，所以如果你赚到超过四十五万kr，最好的选择就是把许可证要求的航程磨到够，然后一步到位买下Selfy。它的航速很快，能够玩到小型和中型船的所有玩法，并且价格还很便宜。

8、要注意的是Selfy虽然能够带一名船员，但如果你只想玩捕蟹，这个船员就对你没有任何作用，他在Selfy上不能帮你摆笼子或回收笼子，也不能分拣公螃蟹和母螃蟹。当然如果你在Selfy上玩延绳钓和渔网，那个船员倒是能发挥出作用，他可以帮你拉绳子、拉网和剖鱼。
另外要注意，只有Selfy的船员不能处理蟹笼，Svalbard上的船员可以帮你摆/回收笼子和分拣帝王蟹。

9、接上一条，虽然中型船的船员确实能帮你剖鱼，但实际上你手动的速度比他做事快很多，所以如果你忙着收好几条延绳，最好的选择还是让他帮忙收延绳或渔网，然后自己动手剖鱼。

edit after ~30 hrs:

I'll keep the "recommended" status on this review. The game has flaws, that's for sure. First of all - not possible to pass time on boat. I mean, come on, some of the boats even have beds!
But that's a minor inconvenience at most, since you can fast travel.

Overall I think the game has a good progression, you start as a lonely fisher on an old boat, keep making money, buying bigger boats (in the end, you're gonna need a bigger boat). Finally you're hauling tons of fish on a single trip, managing a crew of 4-5 and making millions. The crew managing part was good, there is a simple leveling and skill system for the crew members. 

For me the best part of the game came with winter - it got really dark, the sea got really rough and the landscape covered with snow. You start the game in August, so the sea is mostly calm. I was wondering if I ever get to see bigger waves - yes, just play (or skip time) until winter!

Pros:
 - sea / wave physics, the boats have a nice feeling (I'm no sailor, so maybe it's a bit arcade-y but I liked it)
 - good selection of boats
 - crew system
 - music and the atmosphere in general
 - pelagic trawler (Lunar Bow) was excellent, really good implementation and everything makes sense once you get the hang of it

Cons:
 - I didn't like the "net hauling" minigame, the "longline" minigame kinda makes sense but the net version felt like a filler
 - disappearing textures, graphical stutter from time to time etc. minor graphics issues. I feel like my machine should be powerful enough to run this one smoothly (I played Elder Ring on MAX settings!!)

Fishing: Barents Sea is a maritime simulation game that offers a surprisingly meditative and technically detailed experience centered around commercial fishing off the coast of Norway. Developed by Misc Games, this title sets itself apart from the usual simulation fare by narrowing its focus to one occupation and doing its best to replicate that profession with realism and atmosphere. Set in the cold, expansive waters of the Barents Sea, players begin with a modest vessel and a simple line-fishing setup, and through a mixture of smart resource management, navigation, skill development, and economic choices, the journey expands into owning a fleet and managing a small fishing empire. It's a niche title, but one that finds power in its quiet dedication to authenticity.

At its best, the game captures the unique rhythm of life at sea. There is a deliberate pacing to every aspect of gameplay—sailing between fishing zones, using sonar to locate schools of fish, deploying equipment, and hauling in your catch. These processes unfold in real time, and while that may initially feel slow or even tedious, it's exactly this realism that makes Fishing: Barents Sea so immersive. There is something profoundly satisfying about carefully setting a line, waiting hours (in-game time) for optimal conditions, and finally pulling up a full haul of cod or pollock. The developers have clearly invested a lot of effort into creating a realistic fishing environment, complete with dynamic weather, accurate port layouts, and fish population simulations that respond to overfishing and seasonal patterns.

Visually, the game delivers a serene and convincing atmosphere. The ocean is rendered beautifully, with dynamic lighting and weather effects that shift from crisp, calm mornings to stormy gray afternoons. The Norwegian coastline is sparsely populated but feels authentic, with small harbors, rugged terrain, and isolated settlements giving the world a sense of grounded place. The ships, too, are modeled in impressive detail, both inside and out. Each vessel you acquire over the course of your journey is more complex than the last, with better engines, larger storage, more advanced equipment, and realistic cockpits you can navigate from first-person perspective. Sound design adds to the immersion with ambient sea noises, the hum of engines, seagulls circling overhead, and the gentle clatter of fish being sorted below deck.

What makes the game compelling, especially for simulation enthusiasts, is its commitment to gradual progression. Starting small and earning money to repair, refuel, and upgrade your ship is rewarding. You're not simply grinding for cash—you’re developing your own efficiency. New fishing methods like netting or longline fishing become available as you level up your skills and acquire better gear, and each one plays differently, with its own techniques and challenges. You also begin to hire crew members, manage their roles, and eventually delegate tasks, bringing light touches of management sim into the mix. There’s a quiet pleasure in mastering this flow—charting a course, monitoring your sonar, positioning correctly, and timing your hauls just right.

However, Fishing: Barents Sea is not without its shortcomings. While the core simulation is strong, the gameplay loop can eventually become repetitive, especially once you’ve unlocked most of the vessels and mastered the fishing techniques. The economic system is functional but shallow, and while port upgrades, repairs, and fuel costs create a bit of pressure early on, they become negligible in the later game. Interactions with the world are minimal—you don’t engage much with other ships, ports, or environmental events beyond fishing. This leaves the game feeling somewhat empty over time. Additionally, AI pathfinding and crew management can be a little clunky, with crew members occasionally bugging out or failing to perform tasks as expected.

Another area that could use more depth is the storytelling or career progression. There’s no overarching narrative or major goals beyond buying bigger boats and catching more fish. For players who thrive on open-ended simulation, this is fine, but for others, the lack of narrative stakes or varied mission types may make the experience feel flat. There's also a lack of environmental feedback or challenge—for example, weather can look dramatic but rarely affects your operations in a way that changes gameplay meaningfully. Mods and DLCs have tried to address some of these issues by adding new ship types, crab fishing, or expanded mechanics, but the base game remains fairly linear in its progression.

Despite these limitations, Fishing: Barents Sea offers a relaxing, oddly captivating simulation experience that stands out in its genre. It succeeds not through spectacle or complexity, but by embracing the steady, quiet, methodical nature of the profession it simulates. It’s a game that asks for patience and offers a kind of zen return on that investment. While it may not appeal to players looking for fast-paced gameplay or rich storytelling, it’s an excellent choice for those who enjoy slow-burn progression, technical realism, and the serene beauty of open water. It's not a game that screams for attention, but rather one that invites you to take a deep breath, listen to the waves, and work the sea on your own time.

But unfortunately, this game is held back by serious flaws that can't be ignored. Despite releasing back in 2018, it's still riddled with bugs and not just small ones. We're talking about game-breaking issues that can crash your session or corrupt your save, costing you hours of progress. For a game that revolves around slow, methodical play, that’s incredibly frustrating.

Worse still, it’s clear the developers have moved on. Don’t expect patches, fixes, or meaningful updates it’s effectively abandoned. What you see is what you get, and what you get is a buggy, unfinished experience that no longer has any development support.

I like the immersion and the progression feel. Learned a lot about commercial fishing through this game.

Fishing: Barents Sea has a lot of potential, and in many ways, it delivers a relaxing and enjoyable fishing experience  nice ship designs, beautiful scenery, and a decent variety of fishing methods, especially with the DLCs. On the surface, it should be a great maritime sim.

But unfortunately, this game is held back by serious flaws that can't be ignored. Despite releasing back in 2018, it's still riddled with bugs  and not just small ones. We're talking about game-breaking issues that can crash your session or corrupt your save, costing you hours of progress. For a game that revolves around slow, methodical play, that’s incredibly frustrating.

Worse still, it’s clear the developers have moved on. Don’t expect patches, fixes, or meaningful updates  it’s effectively abandoned. What you see is what you get, and what you get is a buggy, unfinished experience that no longer has any development support.

🎣 Nice concept
🚢 Great ship variety (with DLC)
🛠️ Broken, buggy, and abandoned

Verdict: I genuinely enjoyed the game for over 20 hours it’s relaxing and has a lot of charm. But after losing over 2 hours of progress to a bug, I just couldn’t justify continuing. A shame, because the foundation is there… it just desperately needed more polish and support.
